target.userland: GNU or BSD; POSIX utility flags only
target.locale: LC_ALL=C for anything that sorts, compares or byte-counts

verified.bash-3.2: yes — the full suite runs green under a real 3.2.57 (nix develop; bash32-run-tests)
verified.bsd-userland: no — the GNU-vs-BSD flag rules below are verified by reading, not by execution. CI's macos legs are the intended proof and are still continue-on-error.

rules.symptom: declare: -A: invalid option, then the script aborts under set -e
rules.replacement: plan_map_set / plan_map_load / plan_map_has / plan_map_keys / plan_map_count / plan_map_clear (plan-map-lib.sh)
rules.note: plan_map_get forks at the call site; use plan_map_load in a loop.

rules.symptom: mapfile: command not found
rules.replacement: arr=(); while IFS= read -r l; do arr+=("$l"); done < <(...)

rules.symptom: bad substitution
rules.replacement: $(printf '%s' "$var" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

rules.symptom: arr[@]: unbound variable instead of the intended output
rules.replacement: ${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"} , or guard with [ "${#arr[@]}" -gt 0 ]
rules.note: No reliable detector: the pattern is only wrong when the array can be empty. Review every new array expansion by hand.

rules.symptom: invalid timeout specification; the read fails instead of polling
rules.replacement: an integer timeout (`read -t 1`), and design the loop so one second of granularity is acceptable
rules.note: This is why a TUI idle animation on the floor ticks at 1s: sub-second polling, and disambiguating a lone ESC from an escape sequence by timeout, are both unavailable.

rules.symptom: stat: illegal option -- c, empty output, so a mode comparison silently fails
rules.replacement: plan_stat_mode / plan_stat_uid (plan-document-lib.sh), or probe once: stat -c works ? -c : -f '%Lp'

rules.symptom: BSD sed requires a backup suffix, so it eats the script as the suffix and then fails
rules.replacement: sed ... "$f" > "$f.new" && mv "$f.new" "$f"

rules.symptom: fails, then dirname "" yields '.', so script_dir becomes the caller's cwd
rules.replacement: a while [ -L "$p" ] loop (see monitor-read.sh), or plan_resolve_symlink

rules.symptom: no such option; with 2>/dev/null the loop silently reads nothing and the caller reports success
rules.replacement: find ... -print and derive the field in the read loop

rules.symptom: illegal option; a NUL-delimited pipeline then yields zero records
rules.replacement: drop the sort from the NUL pipeline, or sort a newline-safe projection

rules.symptom: emits a literal 'N', so an id keeps its shape while losing all entropy
rules.replacement: date +%s plus $RANDOM$RANDOM

rules.symptom: matches nothing, so a check passes vacuously — worse with || true
rules.replacement: tr -c 'A-Za-z0-9_' '\n' then grep -x, which emulates a word boundary exactly

rules.symptom: unknown option
rules.replacement: sed -E, which both GNU and BSD accept

rules.breaks: unspecified in POSIX; BSD has differed
rules.symptom: copies the wrong thing, or dotfiles are handled differently
rules.replacement: (cd src && tar cf - .) | (cd dst && tar xf -)

rules.breaks: not portable across shells or /bin/echo builds
rules.symptom: prints the flag literally, or fails to interpret escapes
rules.replacement: printf

rules.construct: wc output interpolated into a message
rules.symptom: BSD wc pads to a fixed width, so a message reads 'ok:       42 bytes'
rules.replacement: pipe through | tr -d ' ' before interpolating
rules.note: Arithmetic comparisons are unaffected; only interpolated text shows the padding.

rules.construct: bare sort on data a user or a test sees
rules.breaks: any host with a non-C locale
rules.symptom: collation differs per developer, so generated row order is not reproducible
rules.replacement: export LC_ALL=C at the top of the script, or LC_ALL=C sort at the call

rules.construct: ps -p $$ -o tty= as a tty probe
rules.symptom: Linux prints '?' for no tty, macOS prints '??', so the guard passes and the following /dev/tty open fails with ENXIO
rules.replacement: [ -t 0 ], then try ( exec 3</dev/tty ) 2>/dev/null, else exec 3<&-

rules.construct: backslash escape inside an awk bracket expression
rules.breaks: undefined in POSIX awk; BSD awk may read it literally
rules.symptom: 'n' becomes strippable whitespace
rules.replacement: [[:space:]] already includes newline; drop the \n

rules.construct: timeout, nproc, free, realpath, tac, base64 -w, head -n -N, xargs -r, getopt, /proc
rules.symptom: command not found, or a silently different result
rules.replacement: ask before introducing any of these; timeout has a gtimeout fallback on macOS

rules.breaks: any host, whenever the text is not ASCII
rules.symptom: truncation mid-UTF-8-sequence, and a wrong truncated/not-truncated verdict
rules.replacement: do all budget arithmetic in one unit and say which in a comment
rules.note: Plan documents are full of multi-byte glyphs (§ 💤 ⏳ ✅ —), so this is not hypothetical.

rules.breaks: the dependency budget, not a platform
rules.symptom: a machine without python3 loses a documented feature
rules.replacement: awk for text, jq for JSON. python3 is development-only (benchmark/, unregistered tests).

rules.breaks: every shell, whenever pipefail is set
rules.symptom: the pipeline reports 141 (SIGPIPE) even though grep matched, so `... && found=1` never runs and an `if` silently takes the wrong branch. A check reports 'not found' for something that is there, and a test passes without asserting.
rules.replacement: capture first, then match the string: out="$(cmd || true)"; case "$out" in *needle*) ... ;; esac
rules.note: grep -q exits on the first match and closes the pipe, so the writer dies of SIGPIPE. The sibling trap is grep -c / grep -v / grep -o exiting 1 when nothing matches, which aborts the script under set -e before any assertion runs; wrap those as { grep -c ... || true; }. The failure is timing-dependent — a writer that finishes before grep -q exits never sees SIGPIPE — which is why it survives in small cases and lies in large ones. A whole-input reader is safe, so `| grep -c PATTERN >/dev/null` is the escape hatch when the pattern must stay a line-scoped regex.

rules.breaks: every bash, whenever set -u is on
rules.symptom: a: unbound variable, reported at the declaration itself
rules.replacement: split the declaration: local a="$1"; local b="$a/x"
rules.note: local declares every name in the statement before evaluating any right-hand side, so the earlier name is already local-and-unset while the later value is expanded.

rules.construct:
x="$(cmd <<'EOF' … an apostrophe in the body … EOF
)"
rules.symptom: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `'', or syntax error near unexpected token `)', reported at a line that is NOT the offending one -- the scanner opens a quote in the here-document body and only fails when it runs out of file, so the line number misdirects.
rules.replacement: keep the here-document out of the command substitution: have the helper write a file or set a global, and read that. Backticks also work, but the global is clearer.
rules.note:
bash 3.2 tracks ' and " through a here-document body when it is inside $( ). It is PARITY, not presence: two apostrophes in the body parse fine, one does not. Independent of delimiter quoting, of layout, of assignment-vs-command, and of whether a function is involved. Backslash-escaping is NOT a workaround -- with a quoted delimiter no escape processing happens, so the backslash lands in the data on every shell. bash 4's recursive $( ) parser fixed it. Verified: `x="$(cat <<'MD'
the unit's own
MD
)"` is a syntax error on 3.2.57 and fine on 5.3. This bites here because plan fixtures are English prose. Locate candidates with `grep -rn '[$](.*<<' --include='*.sh'`, then check quote parity of each body; all four current sites are even-parity and safe, but one added apostrophe breaks them.

rules.construct: a quote character inside ${...} — ${var//$'"'/…}, or a quoted replacement ${var//pat/"$repl"}
rules.symptom: bash: bad substitution: no closing `}' — printed with the expansion truncated at the quote, so the reported text is not what you wrote; or, for a quoted replacement, NO error at all and the quote characters land in the data.
rules.replacement: hold the quote in a plain variable and expand it UNQUOTED inside the braces — q='"'; out="${v//$q/\\$q}" behaves identically on 3.2.57 and 5.3.9 — or run the substitution through sed/awk when several passes are needed (context_json_escape_file in plan-context.sh does the three-pass JSON string escape that way).
rules.note: Two defects, one cause: bash 3.2 does not track quoting inside ${ }; bash 4 fixed both. Same family as heredoc-quote-in-command-substitution. (1) PARSE ERROR — an ANSI-C $'…' that yields a QUOTE character ends the scan early. Verified on 3.2.57 vs 5.3.9: with v='a"b', the line printf '%s' "${v//$'"'/X}" prints aXb on 5.3.9 and dies on 3.2.57 with: bad substitution: no closing `}' in "${v//"/X}". ${v#$'"'} fails the same way, so it is not specific to //. It is the quote CHARACTER, not $'…' — $'\n' and $'\t' are fine on 3.2, and a single quote breaks it too. ${v:-$'"'} fails on BOTH shells, so that form is a plain bug, not a portability question. (2) SILENT WRONG DATA — a quoted REPLACEMENT is never unquoted on 3.2. Verified: with v='a.b' and dash='-', "${v//./"$dash"}" is a-b on 5.3.9 and a"-"b on 3.2.57. No error, wrong output. A quoted PATTERN is fine on both ("${v//"."/$dash}" is a-b everywhere), so only the replacement side diverges. The detector covers (1) only; (2) cannot be grepped without false positives — review every ${var//…/…} whose replacement is quoted.
